loText: Explain how risks related to the use of third parties can arise and describe characteristics of an effective third-party risk management framework.
question: A senior risk analyst at a UK general insurer is mapping the supply chain behind its outsourced policy-document printing. The insurer contracts directly with PrintCo. PrintCo has designated a central intermediary, StaffHub, to run the procurement support for the contract, and StaffHub in turn hires individual contractors who work on the insurer’s procurement function. The insurer has no contract with StaffHub or with the contractors. Which classification is most accurate?

options.A: PrintCo is a third party, StaffHub is a fourth party, and the contractors hired by StaffHub are fifth parties within the reach of TPRM.
options.B: PrintCo is a third party, and StaffHub and its contractors are both fourth parties, because they all work under the same provider.
options.C: PrintCo is a third party and StaffHub is a fourth party, but the contractors fall outside TPRM because the insurer has no contract with them.
options.D: StaffHub is a third party because its work supports the insurer’s own contract, and the contractors it hires are fourth parties.

solution:
Senior analyst at a UK insurer classifying a printing provider, its designated intermediary and the intermediary’s contractors.

**Concept and theory**

A firm’s exposure does not stop at the providers it contracts with directly. Those providers use their own suppliers and subcontractors, who use theirs. The source names the layers:

| Layer | Who they are |
|---|---|
| Third party | The firm’s own provider (vendor, supplier, partner, contractor, service provider) |
| Fourth party | A third party of the third party: subcontractors of service providers, suppliers of suppliers |
| Fifth party | Less frequently, the suppliers of the suppliers of the suppliers |

The source’s own illustration of a fifth party is close to this stem: contractors of the service provider (the third party), hired by a central intermediary designated by the service provider (the fourth party), working in support of the procurement function of a large bank. The conclusion drawn is that TPRM rapidly touches the entire supply chain of the organisation. A missing direct contract does not take a party out of TPRM; it only changes the tools (for example, cascading standards through the third party’s contract).

question: A risk consultant is advising an Australian asset manager that is redesigning its operational risk taxonomy. The head of operational risk wants to know where third-party risk sits in the main reference taxonomies. Which of the following statements is most accurate?

options.A: Basel treats third-party failure as a level 1 event type in its own right, while the ORX taxonomy places it at level 2 under process management.
options.B: Basel treats third-party failure as a level 2 category under the event type Clients, Products and Business Practices.
options.C: The revised ORX taxonomy places third-party risk at level 2, so firms that treat TPRM as a level 1 category depart from industry practice.
options.D: Basel treats third-party failure as a level 2 category under Execution, Delivery and Process Management, while ORX and many firms treat it as level 1.

solution:
Risk consultant advising an Australian asset manager on where third-party risk sits in the Basel and ORX taxonomies.

**Concept and theory**

Risk taxonomies arrange operational risk in levels: level 1 is the broad category, level 2 the subcategory beneath it. The Basel taxonomy has seven level 1 event types. The seventh is Execution, Delivery and Process Management (EDPM), and “third-party failure” is recorded as a level 2 category under it (together with other process-related sub-categories).

Third-party risk has grown so much in importance that, for many institutions, TPRM is now a level 1 category of operational risk, with specific risk management practices of its own. The industry body ORX, in its revised operational risk taxonomy, also places third-party risk at level 1.

| Taxonomy | Level | Parent |
|---|---|---|
| Basel event types | Level 2 (“third-party failure”) | EDPM, seventh event type |
| ORX revised taxonomy | Level 1 | None (own category) |
| Many institutions | Level 1 | None (own category) |

**Applying it to this question**

Three facts decide it: the Basel level (2), the Basel parent (EDPM), and the ORX and industry level (1). Only one option has all three right.

**Fragile fact.** Basel: level 2 “third-party failure” under EDPM (event type 7). ORX revised taxonomy and many firms: level 1.

question:
The chief compliance officer of a US regional bank is reviewing a proposal to outsource customer call-centre work and account aggregation to a FinTech located in another country, whose local data privacy rules differ from US rules. Key terms of the proposal are shown below.

| Item | Proposal |
|---|---|
| Annual fee | USD 4.2 million |
| Expected cost saving | 18% of current in-house cost |
| Contract term | 5 years |
| Provider location | Outside the United States |

Which of the following assessments is most accurate?

options.A: Because the work is done abroad, the provider’s local laws on record retention, sanctions and data privacy replace the US requirements for the outsourced activity.
options.B: The proposal adds country, compliance and legal risk, and the bank must still meet all US rules on record retention, sanctions, consumer protection and data privacy.
options.C: The proposal adds country risk, but compliance and legal risk are unchanged because the contract assigns all regulatory compliance to the provider.
options.D: The proposal adds compliance and legal risk only where local laws are stricter than US laws; where they are weaker, the bank faces country risk alone.

solution:
CCO of a US regional bank assessing outsourcing of call-centre and account aggregation work to a foreign FinTech.

**Concept and theory**

Over recent decades financial firms have outsourced more and more core processes: loan and deposit processing, electronic funds transfer, payroll, merchant processing, mortgage servicing, treasury management and customer call centres. Many banks also use third parties, particularly FinTechs, to implement new business applications such as electronic bill payment, account aggregation and digital certification. These providers and their staff are often located in another country.

Outsourcing to a company in a different legal jurisdiction brings three risks at once:

| Risk | Why it arises |
|---|---|
| Country risk | The provider and its staff are located in another country |
| Compliance risk | The bank must still comply with all home-country laws and regulations |
| Legal risk | Home and host rules may interact and conflict |

The source’s example is a US bank using a foreign provider: it must still comply with all US laws and regulations, including record retention, national sanctions, consumer protection and data privacy laws, some of which may conflict with those in the provider’s location. Outsourcing moves the work, not the bank’s legal obligations.

**Concept and theory**

|---|---|---|

The logic of the order is simple: decide whether to outsource, then choose and vet the provider, then formalise the relationship, then watch it, then fix or end it.

I. Third-party evaluation and due diligence play a role comparable to customer due diligence in anti-money laundering risk management.

II. To simplify and standardise due diligence, the insurer uses standard assessment questionnaires such as the SIG questionnaires.

III. Because standard questionnaires are used, every vendor receives the same depth of review and proportionality no longer applies.

IV. Due diligence on a new vendor is completed after the contract is signed, so that it covers the services actually being delivered.

Which of the statements reflect good practice?

options.A: I and II only
options.B: I, II and III only
options.C: II and IV only
options.D: I, II and IV only

The second life-cycle stage is evaluation, risk rating and due diligence. The source makes three points about it:

2. **Standardisation.** To simplify and standardise due diligence, more and more companies use standard assessment questionnaires. The SIG questionnaires provided by Shared Assessments are commonly used.

Due diligence is the gateway to a new relationship, and the next stage states that contracts should be signed only after the assessment and remediation of all remaining open items or issues. options.A: The rating criteria, thresholds, and the due diligence and controls attached to each tier must be consistent with the bank’s overall risk appetite.
options.B: A vendor that can be substituted immediately should be rated higher risk, because a vendor that is easy to replace is likely to be replaced at short notice.

A vendor rating scheme is only useful if it is anchored to how much risk the firm is willing to take. The source states that the risk-rating criteria, the thresholds, and the corresponding due diligence and controls must be in line with the company’s overall risk appetite. This links stage 2 back to stage 1: the business model decision is itself tied to risk appetite, and the rating scheme translates that appetite into concrete thresholds (which vendors count as critical) and concrete responses (how much due diligence, which controls).

- it uses several criteria (process criticality, data access, system access, sector regulation, substitutability), not one;
- substitutability works inversely: the harder a vendor is to replace, the higher the risk;
- ratings are not frozen: continuous monitoring requires reassessment on trigger events (incidents, changes in business circumstances, legal or regulatory changes, changes in services, Acts of God, performance failures).

question: A risk consultant is reviewing a Singapore bank’s plan to move customer records to a public cloud platform under a SGD 40 million, five-year programme. To illustrate what went wrong at Capital One, the consultant prepares a slide on the role of encryption in that breach. Which of the following statements best describes the encryption point in the Capital One case?

options.A: The data was encrypted, but weakly, so the attacker could read it; the lesson is to impose stronger encryption standards on cloud vendors.
options.B: The data was left unencrypted by an improper configuration of the provider’s platform; the lesson is that encryption sits with the cloud provider.
options.C: Neither firm knew of the vulnerability before the attack; the lesson is that encryption offers no protection against unknown attack types.
options.D: Both firms knew of the vulnerability, and encryption would have made the data useless; it was unencrypted because of the bank’s own configuration.

solution:
Risk consultant reviewing a Singapore bank’s cloud plan, explaining the encryption point in the Capital One case.

**Concept and theory**

Encryption is a compensating control: it does not stop an intruder getting in, but it makes what the intruder takes unreadable and therefore useless. That is why it matters most when a known vulnerability cannot be removed immediately. GARP’s account of Capital One builds the lesson in three steps:

1. Capital One and AWS knew their systems were vulnerable to server-side request forgery (SSRF) attacks, of which this attack was one.
2. An effective response to that known vulnerability would have been to encrypt the data, making it useless to attackers.
3. The stolen data was not encrypted, and GARP attributes this to the improper configuration of Capital One’s systems.

After the breach the bank immediately addressed the bug, verified there were no other improper configurations in its environment, and altered its automated scanning to look regularly for the issue. The TPRM lesson is about actors: the vulnerability was known, the remedy was available, and the configuration failure sat with the client institution, not with the provider.

Which response by the CRO is most consistent with the lessons drawn from the Capital One case?

options.B: Providers build strong security into their offerings, so responsibility for monitoring, backups and maintenance passes to the provider once clear service levels are signed.
options.C: Cloud breaches mainly reflect weaknesses in the providers’ own platforms, so the bank should select the provider with the strongest built-in controls and rely on them.

**Concept and theory**

Cloud outsourcing is often treated as if buying a strong platform buys security. GARP uses the Capital One case to correct that view. Two statements carry the lesson. First: even though the major cloud service providers have built strong security into their offerings, it is still the business’s responsibility to handle risk management, monitoring, backups and maintenance. Second, specialists attribute the rise in breaches involving cloud databases and services to poor security hygiene: all the major providers offer the controls needed to keep data in cloud storage private, but customers need to use them.

The division of labour is therefore:

| Cloud provider | Client institution (the bank) |
|---|---|
| Builds strong security into its platform | Keeps risk management, monitoring, backups and maintenance |
| Offers privacy controls for stored data | Must configure and actually use those controls |

This is the cloud-specific form of the wider lesson that accountability for outsourced risk does not leave the client institution.

Which of the following sentences should the analyst include?

options.A: The OCC acted because the bank failed to notify affected customers promptly once it had detected the intrusion into its cloud environment.
options.B: The OCC acted because the cloud provider failed to vet the former employee who carried out the intrusion, and the bank was liable for the provider.
options.C: The OCC acted because the bank failed to establish effective risk assessment processes before migrating significant IT operations to the public cloud.
options.D: The OCC acted because the bank failed to remediate the misconfiguration after the breach, and the same weakness was later found elsewhere in its systems.

Compliance analyst at a Japanese trust bank summarising why the OCC fined Capital One USD 80 million.

**Concept and theory**

Regulators fine banks for what the bank failed to do, and the timing of the failure matters. In the Capital One case the US banking regulator, the Office of the Comptroller of the Currency (OCC), fined the bank USD 80 million. In its released statement the OCC said the action was motivated by the bank’s “failure to establish effective risk assessment processes prior to migrating significant information technology operations to the public cloud environment.”

Three features of this finding are worth fixing:

- Who failed: the bank, not the cloud provider and not the individual attacker.
- What failed: risk assessment processes, a TPRM and governance failure rather than a single technical error.
- When: before the migration of significant IT operations to the public cloud, that is, well before the breach.

By contrast, the bank’s response after the breach was prompt: it immediately addressed the bug, verified there were no other instances of improper configuration, and altered its automated scanning to look for the issue regularly.

**Concept tested:** classification within the four named stability challenges. Intuition: single point of failure in the supply chain = operational risk. The other three challenges are behavior (volatility/speed), visibility (opacity), and attack/abuse (cyber/manipulation).

**Solution:** (a) is correct. Provider failure exposure is the operational-risk challenge: dependence on a small set of third-party AI service providers.

loText: Assess the potential implications of AI for financial stability, with a focus on the following vulnerabilities: - Third-party dependencies and service provider concentration - Market correlations - Cyber risks - Model risk, data, and governance - Other vulnerabilities, such as fraud, disinformation, and misalignment
question: A bank relies on an external provider for its core GenAI capability. Which set of expectations best reflects the third-party risk management standards described in the reading?

options.A: Conduct periodic risk assessments, maintain detailed vendor inventories, and perform ongoing monitoring and due diligence.
options.B: Rely on the provider's industry certifications in place of the bank's own assessments.
options.C: Perform a single comprehensive assessment at onboarding, after which monitoring is unnecessary.
options.D: Contractually transfer accountability for model behavior to the cloud service provider.

solution:
**Concept tested:** third-party risk mitigation expectations. Intuition: a rented engine still gets serviced on the renter's schedule: assess periodically, inventory the vendors, monitor continuously.

**Solution:** (a) is correct. Periodic assessments, vendor inventories, and ongoing monitoring/due diligence are the stated expectations.

loText: Describe characteristics of cyber risks and information/communication technology (ICT) risks faced by financial institutions.
question: Which statement about the limits of risk transfer to cloud service providers is most consistent with the reading?

options.A: Cloud computing moves some, but not all, of an organization's cyber risks to cloud service providers, because the organization's own providers and customers might not always have adequate controls.
options.B: Cloud computing transfers all of an organization's cyber risk to the provider, which is the primary reason for adoption.
options.C: Cloud computing transfers no cyber risk, since the organization retains full custody of its data.
options.D: Climate change and rising energy costs are expected to reduce the frequency and duration of outages.

solution:
Concept tested: the partial nature of risk transfer plus the outage trend. Intuition: you can outsource the servers but not the whole chain; weak links remain among your own suppliers and customers.

(a) is correct. Partial transfer, limited by control weaknesses among the organization's providers and customers.

loText: Describe best practices for regulators pertaining to AI, including the use of AI by supervisors and recommendations for policy on the use of AI by regulated entities.
question: A policy adviser at a Brazilian securities regulator is drafting a gap analysis against the key focus areas that standard-setting bodies have set out in responding to AI applications. Each of the following names focus areas on that list EXCEPT:

options.A: Governance of AI use, and transparency and explainability.
options.B: Outsourcing practices, and data quality and bias.
options.C: Reporting requirements, and maintaining meaningful human oversight.
options.D: Presuming outsourced AI riskier, and ending human oversight.

solution:
**Step 1 – The six focus areas**

Governance of AI use; transparency and explainability; outsourcing practices; data quality and bias; reporting requirements; maintaining meaningful human oversight.

**Step 2 – Find the option that is not on the list**

A, B and C between them name all six. D pairs two positions the reading rejects: there is no indication that outsourced models are riskier than internally developed ones, and maintaining meaningful human oversight is itself a focus area (Schweser Module Quiz 100.3, Question 1, wrong options C and A).

⇒ D is the exception.

**Interpretation**

Outsourcing is a focus because institutions stay fully responsible for what they buy, not because bought models are presumed worse, and human oversight is to be maintained, not phased out. The risk the reading does attach to outsourcing is concentration: reliance on a few third-party providers (CI-1 c).

**LO:** CI-1 d: Describe best practices for regulators pertaining to AI, including the use of AI by supervisors and recommendations for policy on the use of AI by regulated entities. • **Reference:** IMF (October 2024); SchweserNotes 2026 Book 5, Reading 100, LO 100.d, Module Quiz 100.3 Q1

loText: Assess the potential implications of AI for financial stability, with a focus on the following vulnerabilities: - Third-party dependencies and service provider concentration - Market correlations - Cyber risks - Model risk, data, and governance - Other vulnerabilities, such as fraud, disinformation, and misalignment
question: The CRO of a Canadian bank that relies on a single cloud service provider for its GenAI models and computing capacity is reviewing the bank’s third-party risk policy. Which of the following assessments is most consistent with the FSB?

options.A: It exposes the bank to supply chain disruptions and cyber events at key vendors, and calls for periodic assessments, vendor inventories and monitoring.
options.B: The provider’s own certifications of its controls can stand in for the bank’s periodic assessments, since the provider is better placed to judge its own risks.
options.C: A thorough assessment at onboarding meets the third-party standards, so ongoing monitoring is needed only if the provider later changes its service terms.
options.D: Provider concentration brings only costs for the bank, since the FSB sees no offsetting benefit for risk management from coordination or technological synergies.

solution:
**Step 1 – What the dependence exposes**

Service provider concentration and third-party dependencies expose institutions to operational risks, including supply chain disruptions and cyber events affecting key vendors.

**Step 2 – What the bank is expected to do**

Institutions are expected to apply third-party risk management standards: periodic risk assessments, detailed vendor inventories, and ongoing monitoring and due diligence.

⇒ A.

**Interpretation**

The standards are the institution’s to apply; the provider’s size does not move the obligation. The FSB also notes an offset: more coordination and technological synergies may make risk management more effective and eﬀicient.

**LO:** CI-2 c: Assess the potential implications of AI for financial stability, with a focus on the following vulnerabilities: Third-party dependencies and service provider concentration; Market correlations; Cyber risks; Model risk, data, and governance; Other vulnerabilities, such as fraud, disinformation, and misalignment. • **Reference:** FSB (November 2024); SchweserNotes 2026 Book 5, Reading 101, LO 101.c

loText: Describe potential macroprudential tools and policy measures that can be used to address cyber risks and ICT risks and explain challenges to the adoption of each one.
question: The head of compliance at a Dutch bank is mapping EU initiatives on digital resilience for the board. Which statement is correct?

options.A: The ESRB has proposed EU-wide coordination of incident reporting; DORA covers ICT third-party risks from cloud computing.
options.B: DORA has proposed EU-wide coordination of incident reporting; the ESRB runs penetration stress tests of EU banks.
options.C: The EU has only recently begun incident reporting and information sharing, under the ESRB’s proposal for a European-wide structure.
options.D: DORA covers penetration stress testing but leaves ICT third-party risks from cloud computing to Sheltered Harbor-type arrangements.

solution:
**Step 1 – The ESRB**

Policies for incident reporting and information sharing have long been in place in the EU. Going a step further, the European Systemic Risk Board has suggested forming a European-wide structure for coordinating incident reporting.

**Step 2 – DORA**

The Digital Operational Resilience Act has provisions to respond to ICT third-party risks associated with cloud computing, and provisions on penetration stress testing.

⇒ ESRB: coordinated reporting. DORA: cloud third-party risk and penetration testing.

**Interpretation**

Attribution questions turn on who did what. Keep the four names apart: ITU (certification and standardisation), ESRB (incident reporting structure), DORA (cloud third-party risk, penetration testing), Sheltered Harbor (US ICT buffer).

**LO:** CI-8 c: Describe potential macroprudential tools and policy measures that can be used to address cyber risks and ICT risks and explain challenges to the adoption of each one. • **Reference:** Martinez, Banco de España (April 2023); SchweserNotes 2026 Book 5, Reading 107, LO 107.c
